title: Indigenous Education (Targeted Assistance) Amendment Bill 2013
portfolio: School Education, Early Childhood and Youth

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: Supported the Indigenous Education (Targeted Assistance) Amendment Bill but criticised it as only a short-term extension, noting the school nutrition program feeds about 5,000 students across more than 65 remote Northern Territory schools and the ARTIE Academy will involve 21 schools and over 1,600 students, while accusing the government of cutting $22 million from the Indigenous Youth Leadership Program only to later re-announce the same funding.

speeches.speaker: Gai Brodtmann
speeches.brief: Supported the Indigenous Education bill, describing Richardson Primary School in her Canberra electorate where 20 per cent of students are Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, and detailed the $583 million Stronger Futures in the Northern Territory partnership's school nutrition program feeding 5,000 students at 67 schools, alongside the ARTIE Academy which grew from six schools in 2009 to help 1,630 Indigenous students complete their education in 2012.

speeches.speaker: Gai Brodtmann
speeches.brief: Continued speaking on the Indigenous Education (Targeted Assistance) Amendment Bill 2013, detailing additional ARTIE program funding for three South East Queensland primary schools and two Townsville high schools, and citing the government's $128 million Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Education Action Plan and a National Plan for School Improvement Indigenous loading worth $40 million for around 1,400 students in 117 Canberra schools.

speeches.speaker: Sharman Stone
speeches.brief: Criticised the Indigenous Education (Targeted Assistance) Amendment Bill 2013 as another one-year, ad hoc funding extension covering the School Nutrition Program for over 5,000 students in 65 Northern Territory schools and 200 additional teachers, and highlighted the committee's unaddressed 2012 recommendations on foetal alcohol spectrum disorder, citing a short film of a 10-year-old boy from Fitzroy Crossing who was born brain-damaged wishing simply to be normal.

speeches.speaker: Deb O'Neill
speeches.brief: Responded to the member for Murray's remarks on foetal alcohol spectrum disorder, stressing it affects all Australian communities, not just Indigenous ones, including her own electorate.

speeches.speaker: Alan Tudge
speeches.brief: Criticised the Indigenous Education (Targeted Assistance) Amendment Bill 2013 as the third consecutive one-year funding extension, noting Labor has been debating school funding reform since 2004, and cited data showing fewer than one in 10 remote students pass the basic year 5 reading benchmark and Queensland remote students are six years behind by year 9, while praising the Cape York Aboriginal Australian Academy's results across four communities including Aurukun.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, citing 2012 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare data showing 1,024 young people in detention on an average night, 53 per cent of them Indigenous, and 14 Indigenous deaths in custody in 2009-10, and detailed a $300 million Indigenous loading over six years for 10,200 South Australian students under the National Plan for School Improvement plus a new $2.4 million grant for the Australian Indigenous Mentoring Experience program in Adelaide's north.

speeches.speaker: Don Randall
speeches.brief: Praised the Clontarf Foundation's sporting-based Indigenous education program, which began at Bentley in Western Australia over 10 years ago and now runs 54 academies nationally at a cost of just over $7,000 per boy, citing a 90.27 per cent retention rate against a national Indigenous average that improved only from 40.1 to 47.2 per cent in 2010, and said New South Wales alone could expand the program to 5,000 more boys for $35 million if federal funding, one-third of the total cost, were approved.

speeches.speaker: Robert Oakeshott
speeches.brief: Supported the bill, arguing the real failure lies in a school funding model with an intolerable link to education outcomes producing gaps of around 30 per cent for Indigenous, poor and rural students, noted more than half of Australia's Aboriginal population lives on the east coast between Sydney and Rockhampton rather than only remotely, and endorsed the Recognise campaign's Long Walk from Melbourne toward Darwin ahead of a referendum on Indigenous constitutional recognition.

speeches.speaker: Peter Garrett
speeches.brief: Responded to the debate, confirming the Indigenous Youth Leadership Program was not cut and funded 210 new scholarships in 2013 plus an additional $12 million for 204 more in 2014, announced the Australian Capital Territory had just agreed to join the National Plan for School Improvement, and reported that in 2013 the Sporting Chance Program will deliver more than $58 million supporting 75 programs and over 13,000 students.
